title: Pentagon releases new UFO videos, decades-old files in fresh transparency drop
byline: ALEXX ALTMAN-DEVILBISS | The National News Desk
excerpt: The 10 new files were added to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, or PURSUE, which began publishing records in May.
content:
by ALEXX ALTMAN-DEVILBISS | The National News Desk

Fri, September 18, 2026 at 7:55 AM

U.S. Navy Chief Warrant Officer Delbert C. Newhouse reported observing and filming a group of bright airborne objects near Tremonton, Utah, on July 2, 1952 and shortly thereafter submitted the footage to the U.S. Air Force. (DoW)

WASHINGTON (TNND) — The Defense Department on Friday released its sixth batch of declassified Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP), or UFO, records as part of the Trump administration’s transparency initiative.

The 10 new files were added to the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters, or PURSUE, which began publishing records in May. They include audio, video and documents from the Department of War and local law enforcement.

The release features digitized footage filmed near Tremonton, Utah, in 1952 by Navy Chief Warrant Officer Delbert C. Newhouse, who reported seeing a group of bright airborne objects. The film was later reviewed by the Air Force’s Project Blue Book, but officials said its limited detail and lack of fixed reference points prevented a conclusive determination.

Also included are two cellphone videos submitted by a Colorado law-enforcement officer in October 2023. The officer described a silent object with flashing red, blue and green lights. The Pentagon’s All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office cautioned that cellphone autofocus and digital processing can distort the apparent shape and movement of distant objects.

Other files include a 1952 presentation by former Project Blue Book head Capt. Edward J. Ruppelt, who said roughly 20% of about 800 cases reviewed by the Air Force remained unexplained after analysis. Ruppelt stressed, however, that the Air Force had not concluded about the phenomenon’s nature or origin.

The batch also includes Defense Intelligence Agency documents tied to the 2008 Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, or AAWSAP, which examined potential future foreign aerospace threats and technologies. One 2010 report reviews spintronics, a field of electronics that uses electron spin and has possible computing and sensor applications.

The most recent PURSUE records were released in August and included reports dating from 1950 to 2026.

Officials stressed the files are labeled “unresolved” because investigators lacked enough information to make a definitive identification — not because they have been linked to extraterrestrial activity.
